The Olympic Games are the world's preeminent international sporting competition, held every two years with alternating Summer and Winter editions since 1896. They have their roots in the ancient athletic festivals of Greece, and the modern Olympics were revived in 1896 as a symbol of peaceful international cooperation and athletic excellence. Today, nearly two hundred nations participate, with millions of viewers worldwide watching athletes showcase human physical achievement across dozens of disciplines, all on a global stage for national pride and cultural exchange.

The ancient Olympic Games were held in Olympia, Greece, from approximately 776 BCE until around 393 CE—nearly twelve hundred years of continuous competition. They began as a single event: a one hundred ninety-two meter foot race. But over time the games expanded to include wrestling, boxing, and the pentathlon, which combined running, jumping, discus, javelin, and wrestling. There were also chariot racing and equestrian events. Winners received olive wreaths and eternal glory. Athletes trained for years and competed naked as a way to honor Zeus, whose sanctuary stood at Olympia. The games were so important to the ancient world that wars actually paused during the Olympic truce to allow safe passage and competition.

The modern Olympics were revived by Pierre de Coubertin, a French aristocrat and educator, who held the first modern games in 1896 in Athens to promote international peace and athletic excellence. That first modern Olympics featured two hundred forty-one athletes from fourteen nations competing in nine sports. Women were excluded entirely. The Winter Olympics began much later, in 1924 in Chamonix, France, to showcase winter sports. The Summer and Winter Games now alternate every two years. By 2024, the Summer Olympics had grown to involve over ten thousand athletes competing in thirty-two sports, while the Winter Olympics feature fifteen sports.

The modern Olympics have been shaped by several historic moments. The 1936 Berlin Olympics were infamously hosted by Nazi Germany. The American athlete Jesse Owens, who was African American, won four gold medals there, directly contradicting Nazi racial ideology. The 1980 Moscow Olympics were boycotted by the United States and sixty-five other nations in protest of the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan. That same year, the Lake Placid Winter Olympics saw what became known as the Miracle on Ice, when the American ice hockey team defeated the heavily favored Soviet team. The 1996 Atlanta Summer Olympics marked an expansion of women's events and saw increasing participation from emerging economies, though security challenges were underscored by a bombing at Centennial Olympic Park.

The International Olympic Committee governs the Games, while the host nation's Olympic Committee organizes the logistics. Sports are divided into Summer events like athletics, swimming, and gymnastics, and Winter events like ice skating, skiing, and ice hockey. The Olympic torch relay symbolizes the passing of the flame from Olympia, uniting ancient tradition with modern pageantry. Host cities invest billions in venues and infrastructure, though the economic impact varies—some cities benefit greatly while others are left with significant debt.

The Olympic motto is Citius, Altius, Fortius, which means Faster, Higher, Stronger. The games promise to unite nations in peaceful competition. In practice, however, the Olympics have been sites of political protest, nationalism, doping scandals, and environmental concerns. The competitive spirit breeds athletic excellence, but it also creates geopolitical rivalry where medal counts become proxies for national prestige. The games have driven technological innovation in track surfaces and swimsuit design. They normalized women's participation in sports, though women's events lagged behind men's for decades, and they provided a platform for athletes to transcend nationality and inspire humanity. Yet the Olympics also exemplify a fundamental tension: they promise peace while serving as a stage for geopolitical display.
